Manasseh's evil reign (verses 1–9)

Young people often long to be independent and to possess wealth and power before they have acquired good judgment.

But early independence can destroy their future comfort and harm others.

It is often far better for young people to remain under the care of parents or guardians until growing experience and wisdom prepare them to make decisions.

Even if they receive fewer immediate indulgences, they may later be thankful for the protection.

Manasseh committed enormous wickedness before the Lord, almost as though he wanted to provoke divine anger.

He became more wicked than the nations the Lord had previously driven out.

He progressed from evil to worse until he was carried captive to Babylon.

The people readily complied with Manasseh's desires.

Some wanted his favor; others found his commands suited their own corrupt inclinations.

When a great community undergoes reform, many people are merely following the advantage of the moment.

Such people fall away quickly under temptation.

God's judgment is announced against Judah (verses 10–18)

This passage announces what will happen to Judah and Jerusalem.

The image describes the city being emptied and left desolate, yet not finally destroyed.

It would be cleaned out and preserved for the Jews to inhabit again later.

Judah would be abandoned for a time, but not forever.

Its outward privileges would be lost, yet individual believers would be preserved even during judgment.

The Lord may reject a community that professes his name while dishonoring him through wrongdoing.

He will never abandon his cause on earth.

The book of Chronicles records Manasseh's repentance and God's acceptance of him.

That should keep us from despairing even over the recovery of very great sinners.

But no one should continue deliberately in sin, assuming repentance and reform can be postponed until a convenient time.

Scripture gives some striking examples of the conversion of notorious sinners so no one will despair.

Yet they are few so no one will presume.

Amon's evil reign and death (verses 19–26)

Amon polluted God's house with idols.

God then permitted his own house to be stained with his blood.

Those who killed him acted wickedly, yet God was righteous in allowing it.

Judah now experienced a remarkable change: from one of its worst kings to one of its best.

Once more the nation was given an opportunity for reform.

Whether the Lord patiently delays judgment on stubborn sinners or ends their lives quickly, all who continue refusing his ways face destruction.

Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
Wicked reign of Manasseh. | (1-9) |
The prophetic denunciations against Judah. | (10-18) |
Wicked reign and death of Amon. | (19-26) |
Verses 1-9
Young persons generally desire to become their own masters, and to have early possession of riches and power. But this, for the most part, ruins their future comfort, and causes mischief to others. It is much happier when young persons are sheltered under the care of parents or guardians, till age gives experience and discretion. Though such young persons are less indulged, they will afterwards be thankful. Manasseh wrought much wickedness in the sight of the Lord, as if on purpose to provoke him to anger; he did more evil than the nations whom the Lord destroyed. Manasseh went on from bad to worse, till carried captive to Babylon. The people were ready to comply with his wishes, to obtain his favour and because it suited their depraved inclinations. In the reformation of large bodies, numbers are mere time-servers, and in temptation fall away.
[2Kgs.21.10-2Kgs.21.18]
Verses 10-18
Here is the doom of Judah and Jerusalem. The words used represent the city emptied and utterly desolate, yet not destroyed thereby, but cleansed, and to be kept for the future dwelling of the Jews: forsaken, yet not finally, and only as to outward privileges, for individual believers were preserved in that visitation. The Lord will cast off any professing people who dishonour him by their crimes, but never will desert his cause on earth. In the book of Chronicles we read of Manasseh's repentance, and acceptance with God; thus we may learn not to despair of the recovery of the greatest sinners. But let none dare to persist in sin, presuming that they may repent and reform when they please. There are a few instances of the conversion of notorious sinners, that none may despair; and but few, that none may presume.
[2Kgs.21.19-2Kgs.21.26]
Verses 19-26
Amon profaned God's house with his idols; and God suffered his house to be polluted with his blood. How unrighteous soever they were that did it, God was righteous who suffered it to be done. Now was a happy change from one of the worst, to one of the best of the kings of Judah. Once more Judah was tried with a reformation. Whether the Lord bears long with presumptuous offenders, or speedily cuts them off in their sins, all must perish who persist in refusing to walk in his ways.

Josiah repairs the temple; the book of the law is found (verses 1–10)

Josiah became king at a young age, as Manasseh had done, yet their lives developed very differently.

This must be attributed to the distinguishing grace of God.

Those who raised Josiah probably also helped shape that difference.

His character was excellent.

If the people had joined his reforms as sincerely as he continued them, wonderful blessings could have followed.

But the people had become deeply corrupt and foolish through idolatry.

To understand Judah's true spiritual condition, we should read not only its historical records but also the writings of prophets who lived at the time.

While the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was discovered and taken to the king.

It appears to have been missing for a long time.

Perhaps it had been carelessly set aside, as some people leave their Bibles neglected in corners.

Or perhaps some idolaters had deliberately concealed it.

God's providential care of Scripture shows how precious it is to him.

Whether or not this was the only surviving copy, the truths it contained seemed new to both king and high priest.

No collection of summaries, extracts or lessons can preserve knowledge of God and his will as reliably as Scripture itself.

We should not be surprised that the people became so corrupt when the law had become scarce.

Those who led them astray probably tried to keep the book away from them.

Possessing many Bibles makes the sin of neglecting Scripture even more serious.

What greater contempt can we show for God than refusing to read his word—or reading it without believing and obeying it?

The holy law teaches us to recognize sin.

The blessed gospel reveals salvation.

When sinners discover the strictness and excellence of God's commands, they begin to ask, “What must I do to be saved?”

The ministers of the gospel point them to Jesus Christ, the fulfillment and goal of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

Josiah consults the prophetess Huldah (verses 11–20)

The law was read before the king.

Those who honor their Bibles most deeply are the people who study them, feed on them daily and let their light direct their steps.

Awareness of sin and divine judgment should lead us to ask how we may be saved, what to expect and how to prepare.

People who truly recognize the seriousness of God's anger cannot remain indifferent to the question of salvation.

Huldah told Josiah what judgments were coming upon Judah and Jerusalem.

Most of the people remained hardened and unrepentant.

But Josiah's heart was tender.

He humbled himself before the Lord.

Those who fear God's judgment most sincerely are less likely to experience its final condemnation.

Although Josiah would be mortally wounded in battle, Henry says he died at peace with God and entered glory.

Whatever suffering faithful people must endure or witness, they will be gathered to the grave in peace and enter the rest God has prepared for his people.

[2Kgs.22.1-2Kgs.22.10]
Chapter 22
Chapter Outline
Josiah's good reign, His care for repairing the temple, The book of the law found.
(1-10)
Josiah consults Huldah the prophetess.
(11-20)
Verses 1-10
The different event of Josiah's early succession from that of Manasseh, must be ascribed to the distinguishing grace of God; yet probably the persons that trained him up were instruments in producing this difference. His character was most excellent. Had the people joined in the reformation as heartily as he persevered in it, blessed effects would have followed. But they were wicked, and had become fools in idolatry. We do not obtain full knowledge of the state of Judah from the historical records, unless we refer to the writings of the prophets who lived at the time. In repairing the temple, the book of the law was found, and brought to the king. It seems, this book of the law was lost and missing; carelessly mislaid and neglected, as some throw their Bibles into corners, or maliciously concealed by some of the idolaters. God's care of the Bible plainly shows his interest in it. Whether this was the only copy in being or not, the things contained in it were new, both to the king and to the high priest. No summaries, extracts, or collections out of the Bible, can convey and preserve the knowledge of God and his will, like the Bible itself. It was no marvel that the people were so corrupt, when the book of the law was so scarce; they that corrupted them, no doubt, used arts to get that book out of their hands. The abundance of Bibles we possess aggravates our national sins; for what greater contempt of God can we show, than to refuse to read his word when put into our hands, or, reading it, not to believe and obey it? By the holy law is the knowledge of sin, and by the blessed gospel is the knowledge of salvation. When the former is understood in its strictness and excellence, the sinner begins to inquire, What must I do to be saved? And the ministers of the gospel point out to him Jesus Christ, as the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
[2Kgs.22.11-2Kgs.22.20]
Verses 11-20
The book of the law is read before the king. Those best honour their Bibles, who study them; daily feed on that bread, and walk by that light. Convictions of sin and wrath should put us upon this inquiry, What shall we do to be saved? Also, what we may expect, and must provide for. Those who are truly apprehensive of the weight of God's wrath, cannot but be very anxious how they may be saved. Huldah let Josiah know what judgments God had in store for Judah and Jerusalem. The generality of the people were hardened, and their hearts unhumbled, but Josiah's heart was tender. This is tenderness of heart, and thus he humbled himself before the Lord. Those who most fear God's wrath, are least likely to feel it. Though Josiah was mortally wounded in battle, yet he died in peace with God, and went to glory. Whatever such persons suffer or witness, they are gathered to the grave in peace, and shall enter into the rest which remaineth for the people of God.

Josiah reads the law and renews the covenant (verses 1–3)

God had told Josiah that Jerusalem's destruction could not now be prevented and that he would escape the coming disaster personally.

Nevertheless, Josiah carried out his duty and left the results with the Lord.

He solemnly called the people to abandon idolatry and serve God with genuine righteousness and holiness.

Most probably followed only outward forms or acted hypocritically.

Yet the reform would still prevent much public wickedness.

Each person remained accountable before God for personal conduct.

Josiah destroys idols (verses 4–14)

What extraordinary wickedness was found in Judah and Jerusalem!

It scarcely seems possible that such practices could flourish where God was known and where his name was honored—in Salem and Zion, where his dwelling place stood.

Josiah had already reigned eighteen years.

He had personally set an excellent example and upheld religion according to God's law.

Yet when he investigated idolatry, he discovered that it reached very deeply and widely.

Both ordinary history and Scripture teach that all genuine godliness and goodness found on earth come through the recreating Spirit of Jesus Christ.

Reform reaches Israel; the Passover is celebrated (verses 15–24)

Josiah extended his reform to the cities of Israel he could reach.

He preserved the grave of the man of God from Judah who had foretold the destruction of Jeroboam's altar.

After the land had been cleansed of the old leaven of idolatry, the people returned to celebrating the feast.

No Passover like this had been held during the previous reigns.

The revival of a neglected ordinance brought holy joy.

God rewarded their zeal in removing idolatry with unusual signs of his presence and favor.

We have reason to think true religion flourished through the rest of Josiah's reign.

Josiah is killed by Pharaoh Neco (verses 25–30)

Reading these events, we must confess that although God's righteousness is as clear and solid as great mountains, his judgments are deep and beyond our understanding.

The reforming king died while he was still useful.

This was a mercy to Josiah because it spared him from seeing the approaching disaster.

But it was a judgment on his people, since his death opened the way for the nation's devastation.

Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim rule wickedly (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.37" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 31–37</reference>)

After Josiah's burial, one disaster followed another.

Within twenty-two years, Jerusalem was destroyed.

Many wicked people perished.

The remaining people were purified.

Josiah's reform had helped raise up others who joined the small number of faithful people, preserving the precious seed of the future church and nation.

Sometimes a short period and people with limited abilities are enough to undo the good for which faithful servants labored over many years.

But, blessed be God, the good work he begins through his regenerating Spirit cannot be undone.

That work withstands every change and temptation.

Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
Josiah reads the law, and renews the covenant. | (1-3) |
He destroys idolatry. | (4-14) |
The reformation extended to Israel, A passover kept. | (15-24) |
Josiah slain by Pharaoh-nechoh.
(25-30)
Wicked reigns of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim. | (31-37) |
Verses 1-3
Josiah had received a message from God, that there was no preventing the ruin of Jerusalem, but that he should only deliver his own soul; yet he does his duty, and leaves the event to God. He engaged the people in the most solemn manner to abolish idolatry, and to serve God in righteousness and true holiness. Though most were formal or hypocritical herein, yet much outward wickedness would be prevented, and they were accountable to God for their own conduct.
[2Kgs.23.4-2Kgs.23.14]
Verses 4-14
What abundance of wickedness in Judah and Jerusalem! One would not have believed it possible, that in Judah, where God was known, in Israel, where his name was great, in Salem, in Zion, where his dwelling-place was, such abominations should be found. Josiah had reigned eighteen years, and had himself set the people a good example, and kept up religion according to the Divine law; yet, when he came to search for idolatry, the depth and extent were very great. Both common history, and the records of God's word, teach, that all the real godliness or goodness ever found on earth, is derived from the new-creating Spirit of Jesus Christ.
[2Kgs.23.15-2Kgs.23.24]
Verses 15-24
Josiah's zeal extended to the cities of Israel within his reach. He carefully preserved the sepulchre of that man of God, who came from Judah to foretell the throwing down of Jeroboam's altar. When they had cleared the country of the old leaven of idolatry, then they applied themselves to the keeping of the feast. There was not holden such a passover in any of the foregoing reigns. The revival of a long-neglected ordinance, filled them with holy joy; and God recompensed their zeal in destroying idolatry with uncommon tokens of his presence and favour. We have reason to think that during the remainder of Josiah's reign, religion flourished.
[2Kgs.23.25-2Kgs.23.30]
Verses 25-30
Upon reading these verses, we must say, Lord, though thy righteousness be as the great mountains, evident, plainly to be seen, and past dispute; yet thy judgments are a great deep, unfathomable, and past finding out. The reforming king is cut off in the midst of his usefulness, in mercy to him, that he might not see the evil coming upon his kingdom: but in wrath to his people, for his death was an inlet to their desolations. ( [2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.37] 2Ki 23:31-37)
[2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.37]
Verses 31-37
After Josiah was laid in his grave, one trouble came on another, till, in twenty-two years, Jerusalem was destroyed. The wicked perished in great numbers, the remnant were purified, and Josiah's reformation had raised up some to join the few who were the precious seed of their future church and nation. A little time, and slender abilities, often suffice to undo the good which pious men have, for a course of years, been labouring to effect. But, blessed be God, the good work which he begins by his regenerating Spirit, cannot be done away, but withstands all changes and temptations.

Jehoiakim comes under Nebuchadnezzar's rule (verses 1–7)

If Jehoiakim had served the Lord, he would not have had to serve Nebuchadnezzar in this way.

Had he accepted his position as a subject and kept his word, his situation need not have become worse.

But he rebelled against Babylon and brought still more suffering upon himself.

Consider how important it is for nations to mourn and turn from the sins of earlier generations, lest they suffer the consequences.

The Lord's warnings will be fulfilled just as surely as his promises unless sinners turn from their wrongdoing through repentance.

Jehoiachin is taken captive (verses 8–20)

Jehoiachin reigned only three months.

Yet this was enough time to show that he walked in the sins of his predecessors and brought upon himself the consequences of their wrongdoing.

His uncle was appointed to govern.

Zedekiah was the final king of Judah.

The judgments that had fallen on the previous three kings should have warned him.

Instead he continued doing evil as they had done.

When people entrusted with the decisions of a nation act foolishly and against the nation's real interests, we should recognize in that conduct the warning of God's displeasure.

Because of a people's sins, the Lord may hide from them the things that would bring public peace.

To fulfill the hidden purposes of his justice, he need only leave people to the blindness of their minds or the desires of their own hearts.

The gradual approach of God's judgments offers sinners time to repent.

It also gives believers time to prepare for coming trouble.

At the same time, it exposes the stubbornness of those who refuse to abandon their sins.

Chapter Outline
Jehoiakim subdued by Nebuchadnezzar. | (1-7) |
Jehoiachim captive in Babylon. | (8-20) |
Verses 1-7
If Jehoiakim had served the Lord, he had not been servant to Nebuchadnezzar. If he had been content with his servitude, and true to his word, his condition had been no worse; but, rebelling against Babylon, he plunged himself into more trouble. See what need nations have to lament the sins of their fathers, lest they smart for them. Threatenings will be fulfilled as certainly as promises, if the sinner's repentance prevent not. ( [2Kgs.24.8-2Kgs.24.20] 2Ki 24:8-20)
[2Kgs.24.8-2Kgs.24.20]
Verses 8-20
Jehoiachin reigned but three months, yet long enough to show that he justly smarted for his fathers' sins, for he trod in their steps. His uncle was intrusted with the government. This Zedekiah was the last of the kings of Judah. Though the judgments of God upon the three kings before him might have warned him, he did that which was evil, like them. When those intrusted with the counsels of a nation act unwisely, and against their true interest, we ought to notice the displeasure of God in it. It is for the sins of a people that God hides from them the things that belong to the public peace. And in fulfilling the secret purposes of his justice, the Lord needs only leave men to the blindness of their own minds, or to the lusts of their own hearts. The gradual approach of Divine judgments affords sinners space for repentance, and believers leisure to prepare for meeting the calamity, while it shows the obstinacy of those who will not forsake their sins.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJerusalem besieged, Zedekiah taken.1–7The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity.8–21The rest of the Jews flee into Egypt, Evil-merodach relieves the captivity of Jehoiachin.22–30
Jerusalem falls and Zedekiah is captured (verses 1–7)

Jerusalem was so strongly defended that its attackers could not capture it until famine weakened the people inside and made resistance impossible.

Jeremiah's prophecy and Lamentations describe these events more fully.

Here it is enough to note how terrible the people's wickedness and suffering had become.

Eventually the city was stormed.

The king, his household and leading officials escaped at night through secret passages.

But those who think they can escape God's judgments deceive themselves just as surely as those who imagine they can resist them.

Zedekiah's fate fulfilled two prophecies that initially appeared contradictory.

Jeremiah said he would be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 32:5; 34:3).

Ezekiel said he would not see Babylon (Ezekiel 12:13).

Both statements came true.

Zedekiah was taken to Babylon, but his eyes had been put out, so he never saw it.

The temple is burned and the people exiled (verses 8–21)

Jerusalem and its temple were burned.

Henry considers it probable that the ark was destroyed in the fire.

This showed how little God values the outward splendor of worship when its living power and reality are neglected.

Jerusalem's walls were demolished.

Its people were carried into captivity in Babylon, and the temple's vessels were taken away.

When the people had rejected the realities the sacred symbols represented, why should the symbols remain?

It was just for God to remove the blessings of true worship from people who had preferred false forms of worship.

Those who had insisted on having many altars would now have none.

God did not spare angels who sinned.

He has appointed death for fallen humanity and judgment for those who refuse to believe.

Nor did he spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.

Therefore we should not be astonished that he brings serious judgments upon guilty nations, churches or individuals.

Gedaliah is killed; Jehoiachin receives relief (verses 22–30)

The king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah as governor and protector of the Jews who remained in the country.

But the people did not recognize the opportunity for peace given to them.

Ishmael treacherously killed Gedaliah and his associates.

The surviving Jews then went to Egypt against Jeremiah's counsel.

Through their folly and disobedience they brought further ruin upon themselves (Jeremiah 40–45).

After thirty-seven years in prison, Jehoiachin was released.

No one should say that good can never return merely because suffering has continued for a long time.

Even people in extreme distress cannot know what change God's providence may yet bring to their circumstances, or what comfort may await them after years of affliction.

Even in this life, the Savior gives freedom from bondage to the distressed sinner who seeks him, granting a foretaste of the pleasures at his right hand forever.

Sin alone can truly harm us; Jesus alone can truly do good to sinners.
classic_reading:
[2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.7]
Chapter 25
Chapter Outline
Jerusalem besieged, Zedekiah taken. | (1-7) |
The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity. | (8-21) |
The rest of the Jews flee into Egypt, Evil-merodach relieves the captivity of Jehoiachin.
(22-30)
Verses 1-7
Jerusalem was so fortified, that it could not be taken till famine rendered the besieged unable to resist. In the prophecy and Lamentations of Jeremiah, we find more of this event; here it suffices to say, that the impiety and misery of the besieged were very great. At length the city was taken by storm. The king, his family, and his great men escaped in the night, by secret passages. But those deceive themselves who think to escape God's judgments, as much as those who think to brave them. By what befell Zedekiah, two prophecies, which seemed to contradict each other, were both fulfilled. Jeremiah prophesied that Zedekiah should be brought to Babylon, [Jer.32.5] Jer 32:5; [Jer.34.3] 34:3; Ezekiel, that he should not see Babylon, [Ezek.12.13] Eze 12:13. He was brought thither, but his eyes being put out, he did not see it.
[2Kgs.25.8-2Kgs.25.21]
Verses 8-21
The city and temple were burnt, and, it is probable, the ark in it. By this, God showed how little he cares for the outward pomp of his worship, when the life and power of religion are neglected. The walls of Jerusalem were thrown down, and the people carried captive to Babylon. The vessels of the temple were carried away. When the things signified were sinned away, what should the signs stand there for? It was righteous with God to deprive those of the benefit of his worship, who had preferred false worships before it; those that would have many altars, now shall have none. As the Lord spared not the angels that sinned, as he doomed the whole race of fallen men to the grave, and all unbelievers to hell, and as he spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, we need not wonder at any miseries he may bring upon guilty nations, churches, or persons.
[2Kgs.25.22-2Kgs.25.30]
Verses 22-30
The king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah to be the governor and protector of the Jews left their land. But the things of their peace were so hidden from their eyes, that they knew not when they were well off. Ishmael basely slew him and all his friends, and, against the counsel of Jeremiah, the rest went to Egypt. Thus was a full end made of them by their own folly and disobedience; see Jeremiah chap. 40 to 45 Jehoiachin was released out of prison, where he had been kept 37 years. Let none say that they shall never see good again, because they have long seen little but evil: the most miserable know not what turn Providence may yet give to their affairs, nor what comforts they are reserved for, according to the days wherein they have been afflicted. Even in this world the Saviour brings a release from bondage to the distressed sinner who seeks him, bestowing foretastes of the pleasures which are at his right hand for evermore. Sin alone can hurt us; Jesus alone can do good to sinners.
